strands.name: Number Sense
strands.description: Subitizing, counting, ten-frames, place value, comparing — building a feel for how numbers live.

strands.name: Add & Subtract Structures
strands.description: Part-whole, change, comparison — the *shapes* of arithmetic, not just the answers.

strands.name: Mystery Numbers
strands.description: Secret-number puzzles that plant the seed of algebra without symbols.

strands.name: Equality & Balance
strands.description: Equals means *the same as*. True/false equations, balance scales, both-sides thinking.

strands.name: Patterns
strands.description: Repeating, growing, function-machine patterns. Predicting and explaining.

strands.name: Logic & Sorting
strands.description: Attribute games, 'is not' clues, ordering puzzles. Reasoning under constraints.

strands.name: Geometry & Space
strands.description: Shapes, symmetry, paper folding, mental rotation, tangram, position words.

strands.name: Measurement
strands.description: Length, time, money, weight — using both standard and child-invented units.

strands.name: Counting Ways
strands.description: How many ways? Outfits, paths, breakdowns of a number — early combinatorics.

strands.name: Math Games
strands.description: Two-player strategy games (Nim, Race-to-100, Pig). Strategy = invariant thinking.

problems.title: How many?
problems.prompt: Sit across from your child at the table. Put two objects out, side by side. Cover with your hand for a second, lift and immediately put your hand back down — your child sees them for about one second. Ask: **"How many?"** Repeat with 3, the
problems.explain_prompt: After 2–3 rounds, ask: **"How did you know?"** The point is not the right number — it's whether they *saw it* (subitizing) or *counted it*. Both are good.
problems.parent_script: Sit across from your child at the table. Put two objects out, side by side. Cover with your hand for a second, lift and immediately put your hand back down — your child sees them for about one second. Ask: **"How many?"** Repeat with 3, then 1, then 4 objects, each time covering between rounds.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "I just knew" → subitizing. Strong sign at this age.
- Counting in the air with a finger → also good, slower but accurate.
- A wrong number → no correction. Try again with the same arrangement.
problems.capture_field: What did they actually say? What did they do with their fingers or eyes?

problems.title: One for me, one for you
problems.prompt: Put 4 cups in a row. Put a pile of spoons next to them. Say: **"Can you give each cup exactly one spoon?"** Watch them work. Don't help unless they ask.
problems.explain_prompt: When they're done: **"Are there enough? How do you know?"** Some kids will physically pair (lifting a spoon over each cup), some will count cups then spoons, some will just look. All valid.
problems.parent_script: Put 4 cups in a row. Put a pile of spoons next to them. Say: **"Can you give each cup exactly one spoon?"** Watch them work. Don't help unless they ask.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Physical one-to-one matching is the foundation skill — more important than counting at this age.
- If they pair correctly but can't explain why, that's fine. The understanding is in the doing.
- Variation: add an extra spoon. "Is there one for every cup?" Now they have to notice the leftover.
problems.capture_field: Did they pair physically or count? Did they notice the extra?

problems.title: Count up to the cookie
problems.prompt: Put 5 raisins on a plate. Tell your child: **"You can eat them all. But first, count them with me. One … two … three … four … five."** Touch each one as you both say the number. Then say: **"Now you count, and I'll touch."**
problems.explain_prompt: After they've counted, ask: **"How many will be left if we eat one?"** Eat one (or let them eat one). Recount together. "How many now?"
problems.parent_script: Put 5 raisins on a plate. Tell your child: **"You can eat them all. But first, count them with me. One … two … three … four … five."** Touch each one as you both say the number. Then say: **"Now you count, and I'll touch."**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Are they pointing/touching one item per number word (one-to-one with the count)?
- Do they say "four" when there are four, or are they reciting numbers without tracking?
- Recounting after eating one — do they know they have to recount, or just say "one less"?
problems.capture_field: Did they get the count right? Did they need to recount or did they know "one less"?

problems.title: More or less?
problems.prompt: Make two piles on the table: one pile of 3, one pile of 6. Ask: **"Which pile has more?"** They'll point. Now make piles of 4 and 5. Ask again. Then make 7 and 2.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know which has more?"** Some kids will say "it looks bigger." Some will count both piles. Some will pair them off one-to-one. Each is a different way of comparing.
problems.parent_script: Make two piles on the table: one pile of 3, one pile of 6. Ask: **"Which pile has more?"** They'll point. Now make piles of 4 and 5. Ask again. Then make 7 and 2.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Visual judgment (looks bigger) works for very different sizes but breaks down for close ones — let them discover this.
- Counting both piles is more advanced.
- One-to-one pairing (lining them up) is the most mature strategy.
problems.capture_field: Which strategy did they use? Did it change when the piles were close in size?

problems.title: Hidden hands
problems.prompt: Hold up 3 fingers behind your back. Bring them out for one second, then hide again. Ask: **"How many fingers?"** Repeat with 2, 4, 1, 5. Mix one and two hands.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you see it so fast?"** This is subitizing on fingers — pre-cursor to instant number sense. By Pre-K end, most kids should subitize 1–4 reliably.
problems.parent_script: Hold up 3 fingers behind your back. Bring them out for one second, then hide again. Ask: **"How many fingers?"** Repeat with 2, 4, 1, 5. Mix one and two hands.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Speed matters here — instant answers indicate subitizing.
- 1–3 fingers should be instant; 4–5 is still developing at this age.
- If they want to count slowly, fine — show fewer fingers so they can succeed at subitizing.
problems.capture_field: Which numbers were instant? Which needed counting?

problems.title: The fingers game
problems.prompt: Say a number from 1 to 5. Your child holds up that many fingers. Then they say a number and you hold up that many. Take turns.
problems.explain_prompt: Pick numbers where they have to *think* — start with 1, 2, 3 (easy) then jump to 4 or 5. After they show 5, ask: **"Can you show 5 a different way?"** Most kids will show one whole hand. Can they show 3+2? 4+1?
problems.parent_script: Say a number from 1 to 5. Your child holds up that many fingers. Then they say a number and you hold up that many. Take turns.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Decomposing 5 into 4+1 or 3+2 is a big developmental moment — usually late Pre-K or K.
- If they always go all-one-hand-then-one, that's developmentally fine; the alternative will come.
problems.capture_field: Did they find different ways to show 5? What were they?

problems.title: Empty cup, full cup
problems.prompt: Show your child a cup. Pour cereal in until it's full. Say: **"This is full."** Pour it back out. **"This is empty."** Now pour halfway. **"What's this?"** They might say "some" or "half."
problems.explain_prompt: **"Can you show me a cup with a little bit? With a lot? With nothing?"** This is the conceptual cousin of zero/few/many before number words attach.
problems.parent_script: Show your child a cup. Pour cereal in until it's full. Say: **"This is full."** Pour it back out. **"This is empty."** Now pour halfway. **"What's this?"** They might say "some" or "half."
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Vocabulary: full, empty, some, little, lot — at Pre-K these are the building blocks of comparison.
- "Half" is sophisticated for Pre-K; many won't have the word but will pour to the right level.
problems.capture_field: What words did they use for "some" or "half"? Did the language surprise you?

problems.title: The cookie monster game
problems.prompt: Put 5 items on a plate. Say: **"There are five cookies. The cookie monster is hungry."** Use your hand as a puppet (chomp sound) and "eat" one. **"How many now?"** Continue: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0.
problems.explain_prompt: After "zero," ask: **"What happens next? Can the monster keep eating?"** This is the conceptual seed of "you can't take from nothing" — but kids will sometimes invent fun answers ("the plate is the next cookie!"), which is great.
problems.parent_script: Put 5 items on a plate. Say: **"There are five cookies. The cookie monster is hungry."** Use your hand as a puppet (chomp sound) and "eat" one. **"How many now?"** Continue: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counting backwards is harder than counting forwards. Stumbling is normal.
- "Zero" / "none" / "all gone" — what word do they reach for?
- Reaching the "nothing left" moment — do they understand it ended, or want to continue?
problems.capture_field: What did they call "zero"? What did they say when there were none?

problems.title: Count the steps
problems.prompt: Walk with your child from the kitchen to the front door (or up the stairs). Count each step out loud together: "One … two … three …" Match the count to the step.
problems.explain_prompt: When you arrive, ask: **"How many steps was that?"** Then walk back and count again. **"Is it the same number? Why?"**
problems.parent_script: Walk with your child from the kitchen to the front door (or up the stairs). Count each step out loud together: "One … two … three …" Match the count to the step.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counting with motion is harder than counting still objects — kids often skip or double.
- Realizing the count is the same both directions is a small but real "conservation" moment.
problems.capture_field: Did they keep their count synced with their feet? What did they say when the count came out different the second time?

problems.title: One more bear
problems.prompt: Line up 2 bears. **"How many bears?"** They say "two." Add one more. **"And now? One more bear — how many?"** Continue: 3, then 4, then 5.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know it's three now?"** Some kids will recount the whole line. Some will just say "three" because they tracked the +1. Both are good.
problems.parent_script: Line up 2 bears. **"How many bears?"** They say "two." Add one more. **"And now? One more bear — how many?"** Continue: 3, then 4, then 5.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Recounting after each addition → developmentally typical, building the count.
- Knowing "one more makes three" without recounting → starting to understand the *structure* of adding.
problems.capture_field: Did they recount each time, or know one more?

problems.title: Hide and find
problems.prompt: Put 5 objects on the table. Have your child count them. Cover with a cloth. Reach under the cloth, take one away, hide it in your hand. Reveal: **"How many now?"** They count: 4. **"What happened?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know one is missing?"** The answer can be "I counted" or "I remember there were five." Either is great.
problems.parent_script: Put 5 objects on the table. Have your child count them. Cover with a cloth. Reach under the cloth, take one away, hide it in your hand. Reveal: **"How many now?"** They count: 4. **"What happened?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Recounting reveals current count but not necessarily the change.
- Saying "you took one" reveals tracking of the action.
problems.capture_field: Did they figure out one was missing by recounting or by memory of the original?

problems.title: The sharing problem
problems.prompt: Put 2 plates out. Give your child 4 raisins. **"Can you share these so each plate has the same?"** Let them work.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know it's fair?"** They might say "I gave one to each" or "two and two." Both reveal different understanding.
problems.parent_script: Put 2 plates out. Give your child 4 raisins. **"Can you share these so each plate has the same?"** Let them work.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Alternating distribution ("one for you, one for me") — the foundation of fair sharing.
- All-on-one-side first, then noticing it's unfair → also great, self-correcting is sophisticated.
- 6 items between 3 plates is the natural next step if this is easy.
problems.capture_field: How did they distribute? Did they count after, or just check by looking?

problems.title: Both hands together
problems.prompt: Hold up 2 fingers on one hand. **"How many?"** Then hold up 3 on the other. **"And here?"** Now put both hands together. **"All together — how many?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you find it? Did you count all of them, or count from where we were?"** "Count on" (saying "two … three, four, five") is more advanced than starting over.
problems.parent_script: Hold up 2 fingers on one hand. **"How many?"** Then hold up 3 on the other. **"And here?"** Now put both hands together. **"All together — how many?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Starting over and counting all 5 → developmentally typical Pre-K.
- Saying "two … three, four, five" — counting on — is early K territory and a meaningful leap.
problems.capture_field: Did they count all from one, or count on from the first number?

problems.title: The empty bowl
problems.prompt: Put 4 objects in a bowl. **"How many in the bowl?"** Now take them all out, one by one, counting down: "three … two … one … zero." Say: **"What's in the bowl now?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"What's zero? Can we have less than zero things in the bowl?"** This question doesn't have a Pre-K-friendly answer (it does, but not without negative numbers) — the *asking* is what matters. Kids invent wonderful answers.
problems.parent_script: Put 4 objects in a bowl. **"How many in the bowl?"** Now take them all out, one by one, counting down: "three … two … one … zero." Say: **"What's in the bowl now?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- The word "zero" / "none" / "nothing" — which do they reach for?
- Their answer to "less than zero" is rarely correct mathematically, but it's a window into how they think about emptiness.
problems.capture_field: What was their answer to "less than zero"? Worth saving verbatim.

problems.title: What's under the cup?
problems.prompt: Show your child 4 objects. Have them count: 4. While they watch, put 2 under one cup and 2 under the other. Lift one cup: 2 under here. **"How many under the other cup? How do you know?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you figure it out?"** This is the missing-addend idea in disguise. 4 total, 2 visible — kid figures the other must be 2.
problems.parent_script: Show your child 4 objects. Have them count: 4. While they watch, put 2 under one cup and 2 under the other. Lift one cup: 2 under here. **"How many under the other cup? How do you know?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "Because four take away two is two" — verbal arithmetic. Late Pre-K.
- "Because they were the same when you split them" — structural memory. Excellent.
- A guess → fine. Reveal both cups. Try again with 5 objects (3+2 or 4+1).
problems.capture_field: Did they reason or guess? If they reasoned — what was the reason?

problems.title: The penny vanished
problems.prompt: Show 3 pennies. Count them with your child: 3. Cover with cloth. While they watch, reach under, palm one (don't reveal it). Lift cloth: **"How many?"** They count: 2. **"What happened?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"Where is the third penny? Can you guess?"** This is a missing-quantity story in narrative form.
problems.parent_script: Show 3 pennies. Count them with your child: 3. Cover with cloth. While they watch, reach under, palm one (don't reveal it). Lift cloth: **"How many?"** They count: 2. **"What happened?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "You took it" (with confidence) → tracking the action.
- A bewildered shrug → fine. Reveal the penny in your hand and laugh.
- Older or quicker kids may want to play the trick on you next.
problems.capture_field: Did they figure out you palmed it? What was their guess?

problems.title: Some animals went home
problems.prompt: Line up 5 animals. **"Five animals at the park."** Make a story: **"Two went home for dinner."** Move 2 away. **"How many are still at the park?"** They count: 3.
problems.explain_prompt: Repeat with different start numbers. Then reverse: **"There are 3 at the park. Some went home. How many went home?"** (Start with 5, end with 3, missing addend = 2.) This is harder — they may need to act it out.
problems.parent_script: Line up 5 animals. **"Five animals at the park."** Make a story: **"Two went home for dinner."** Move 2 away. **"How many are still at the park?"** They count: 3.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Forward stories (start 5, take away 2, find 3) are accessible.
- Backward stories (3 left, find how many went) are the seed of algebra and may be too hard. Acting it out is the bridge.
problems.capture_field: Did the backward story make sense? What did they say when stuck?

problems.title: Same or different?
problems.prompt: Make two small piles in front of your child: 3 pennies on the left, 3 pennies on the right. **"Are these the same or different?"** They say "same." Now make 3 on the left and 4 on the right. **"And now?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know?"** Counting both is one answer. Pairing them off (one on left next to one on right) is another. Either works.
problems.parent_script: Make two small piles in front of your child: 3 pennies on the left, 3 pennies on the right. **"Are these the same or different?"** They say "same." Now make 3 on the left and 4 on the right. **"And now?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counting each pile separately → mature.
- Pairing physically → also mature, possibly more intuitive at this age.
- Just visual judgment → fine when piles are very different sizes; will fail when they're close.
problems.capture_field: How did they check? Did they count or pair?

problems.title: Make them match
problems.prompt: Put 4 objects in front of you. **"I have four. Can you make a pile that's the same as mine?"** Let them work. When done, ask: **"Is yours the same as mine? How do you know?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"Can you show me, without counting, that they're the same?"** Pair them off. This is the foundation of equality-as-relation rather than equality-as-computed-result.
problems.parent_script: Put 4 objects in front of you. **"I have four. Can you make a pile that's the same as mine?"** Let them work. When done, ask: **"Is yours the same as mine? How do you know?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counting their pile and stopping at 4 → counting strategy.
- Putting one of theirs next to each of yours → pairing strategy. Same answer, different concept.
problems.capture_field: Counting or pairing? Did they trust their answer?

problems.title: Fair share
problems.prompt: Give your child 6 raisins and 2 plates. **"Share them fairly between the two plates. Each plate gets the same."** Let them work.
problems.explain_prompt: When done, ask: **"How do you know it's fair?"** Counting each plate, or pairing the plates by lifting one raisin from each — both are valid.
problems.parent_script: Give your child 6 raisins and 2 plates. **"Share them fairly between the two plates. Each plate gets the same."** Let them work.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Alternating distribution — strong.
- Counting after distributing to check — also strong.
- Try 8 raisins next, then 5 (uneven). What do they do with the leftover?
problems.capture_field: How did they handle the leftover with 5 raisins?

problems.title: The scale game
problems.prompt: Show them the scale. Put a heavy object in one side (a small can) and a light object (a feather, a paper square) in the other. **"Which side is heavier? How do you know?"**
materials: A coat hanger + 2 paper cups with string  OR a real kitchen scale
problems.explain_prompt: **"Can you make the two sides the same?"** They'll have to add more light objects until the scale balances — a physical equality.
problems.parent_script: Show them the scale. Put a heavy object in one side (a small can) and a light object (a feather, a paper square) in the other. **"Which side is heavier? How do you know?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They understand heavier = lower side / lighter = higher side.
- They iterate: add objects, observe, add more. This is the foundation of "balance both sides."
- The leap from "heavier" to "equal" is the equality concept in physical form.
problems.capture_field: Did they figure out how to balance it? How many tries?

problems.title: Red, blue, red, blue
problems.prompt: Build a pattern: **red, blue, red, blue, red, blue.** Point past the last one and ask: **"What comes next?"** Keep going as long as they're engaged. Then build a different pattern (blue-blue-red, blue-blue-red) and start over.
problems.explain_prompt: **"What did you notice?"** or **"What's the rule?"** The leap from predicting the next piece to articulating the rule is a big developmental step.
problems.parent_script: Build a pattern: **red, blue, red, blue, red, blue.** Point past the last one and ask: **"What comes next?"** Keep going as long as they're engaged. Then build a different pattern (blue-blue-red, blue-blue-red) and start over.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Correct predictions, no articulation → very common at Pre-K. The pattern is felt, not yet spoken.
- A wrong rule that's internally consistent ("red-blue-red-blue-red") → fascinating. Let them follow it.
problems.capture_field: Did they say the rule, or just predict? In what words?

problems.title: The clap-stomp pattern
problems.prompt: Sit facing your child. **"Watch and listen. Clap, stomp, clap, stomp, clap, stomp."** Do it slowly with sound. Then: **"Your turn — clap, stomp, clap, stomp …"** Let them continue. Then try a harder one: **"Clap, clap, stomp, clap, clap, st
problems.explain_prompt: **"Can you make up your own pattern?"** This is the inversion — they invent, you follow. Most Pre-K kids love being the leader.
problems.parent_script: Sit facing your child. **"Watch and listen. Clap, stomp, clap, stomp, clap, stomp."** Do it slowly with sound. Then: **"Your turn — clap, stomp, clap, stomp …"** Let them continue. Then try a harder one: **"Clap, clap, stomp, clap, clap, stomp."**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Audio/motor patterns are often easier than visual ones at this age.
- Can they extend? Can they invent? Two different skills.
- Invented patterns are sometimes irregular — that's information about their concept of "rule."
problems.capture_field: Could they invent a pattern? What did it sound like?

problems.title: Big-small-big-small
problems.prompt: Lay out: **big, small, big, small, big.** **"What comes next?"** Then try: **big, big, small, big, big, small.**
materials: Two sizes of any object — big
problems.explain_prompt: **"How is this pattern different from the red-blue one?"** (If you've done it.) Or simply: **"What's the rule here?"** Size patterns require attending to a different attribute than color.
problems.parent_script: Lay out: **big, small, big, small, big.** **"What comes next?"** Then try: **big, big, small, big, big, small.**
problems.what_to_listen_for: - Some kids handle color easily but get tangled in size. Same skill, different attribute — info about *which attributes they're tracking*.
problems.capture_field: Was size harder than color? Why?

problems.title: Up-down-up-down
problems.prompt: Hold the puppet. **"Up, down, up, down, up …"** Move the puppet each time you say it. **"What comes next?"** Then: **"Up, up, down, up, up, down."**
problems.explain_prompt: **"Can you do the pattern with me?"** They mirror. Then they lead, you follow.
problems.parent_script: Hold the puppet. **"Up, down, up, down, up …"** Move the puppet each time you say it. **"What comes next?"** Then: **"Up, up, down, up, up, down."**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Spatial-language patterns are useful precursors to graphing and number-line work later.
- Many kids can do this physically before they can describe it.
problems.capture_field: Did they lead well? What words did they use?

problems.title: Three-color pattern
problems.prompt: Build: **red, blue, yellow, red, blue, yellow, red, blue …** **"What comes next?"** Three-element patterns are harder than two-element. Some Pre-K kids handle it, some don't yet.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you know yellow comes after blue?"** Some will articulate the cycle; some will just feel it.
problems.parent_script: Build: **red, blue, yellow, red, blue, yellow, red, blue …** **"What comes next?"** Three-element patterns are harder than two-element. Some Pre-K kids handle it, some don't yet.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- If they confidently predict, great.
- If they break the pattern (red after yellow instead of red after the cycle), they're tracking by "the color before" rather than the whole cycle. That's a discovery moment.
problems.capture_field: Did they handle three colors, or stick to thinking in twos?

problems.title: The growing snake
problems.prompt: Build a row of 1 block. Next to it, a row of 2. Next to that, a row of 3. **"Look at our snake — what do you notice?"** Build a row of 4. **"What comes next?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How is each row different from the one before it?"** "One more" is the answer. Whether they articulate it or just continue building it.
problems.parent_script: Build a row of 1 block. Next to it, a row of 2. Next to that, a row of 3. **"Look at our snake — what do you notice?"** Build a row of 4. **"What comes next?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They continue the pattern by adding one each time → strong intuitive grasp.
- They build a random next row → no pattern grasp yet, totally normal for Pre-K.
- "One more!" said aloud → developmental win.
problems.capture_field: Did they continue the +1 pattern? Could they say what was happening?

problems.title: Pattern in the kitchen
problems.prompt: Walk around the kitchen with your child. **"Can we find a pattern somewhere?"** Point to floor tiles, fabric patterns, the spice rack, anything that repeats. Each time you spot one, describe it: "Big tile, small tile, big tile, small tile."
problems.explain_prompt: **"Can you find a pattern I haven't shown you?"** They become the pattern-spotter.
problems.parent_script: Walk around the kitchen with your child. **"Can we find a pattern somewhere?"** Point to floor tiles, fabric patterns, the spice rack, anything that repeats. Each time you spot one, describe it: "Big tile, small tile, big tile, small tile."
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Real-world patterns are usually richer than constructed ones (3+ attributes at once).
- Finding their own pattern is the goal — even if it's not technically a perfect repeat.
problems.capture_field: Where did they find one? What did they call it?

problems.title: Make your own
problems.prompt: Hand your child a small collection of mixed objects. **"Can you make a pattern? Any pattern you want."** When they do, ask: **"What's your rule? Can you keep it going?"**
problems.explain_prompt: Then: **"Can you make a different pattern with the same things?"** Inventing a pattern is harder than continuing one. Inventing two different ones is harder still.
problems.parent_script: Hand your child a small collection of mixed objects. **"Can you make a pattern? Any pattern you want."** When they do, ask: **"What's your rule? Can you keep it going?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Invented patterns are sometimes just "arrangements" without a rule. That's fine — gently prompt: "What comes after the green block?"
- Two different patterns from the same objects → exceptional Pre-K abstraction.
problems.capture_field: What patterns did they invent? Were they truly repeating, or just arrangements?

problems.title: Which one doesn't belong?
problems.prompt: Lay out 4 objects. **"Which one doesn't belong?"** Whatever they pick, don't react. Ask: **"Why?"**
materials: 4 objects with multiple defensible "doesn't belong" answers
problems.explain_prompt: After their first answer: **"Can you find a different one that doesn't belong, for a different reason?"** Every object can be the odd one out for some reason.
problems.parent_script: Lay out 4 objects. **"Which one doesn't belong?"** Whatever they pick, don't react. Ask: **"Why?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They flip and pick a different one for a different reason → abstract reasoning happening in real time.
- They invent an unusual category ("this one is the only one I don't like") → fine. They're using categories.
problems.capture_field: What reasons did they give? Did the second one surprise you?

problems.title: Sort by color
problems.prompt: Mix the objects in a pile. **"Can you put all the same colors together?"** Let them sort.
problems.explain_prompt: When done: **"How did you decide which go together?"** "By color" is the answer they may or may not articulate.
problems.parent_script: Mix the objects in a pile. **"Can you put all the same colors together?"** Let them sort.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Sorting silently — they understand attribute, may not have the word.
- Sorting and naming colors — strong.
- Mistakes (a blue-green item into the blue pile) → fine. Categories are fuzzy in the real world.
problems.capture_field: Did they articulate "color" as the rule? Any boundary cases?

problems.title: Sort by size
problems.prompt: Lay out a mix of sizes. **"Can you sort these?"** Don't tell them by what — see what they do.
materials: Same kind of object in 2–3 sizes
problems.explain_prompt: After they sort by size: **"Could you sort them another way?"** Most Pre-K kids will look stuck. If they came up with color first, prompt size. The discovery that *one set has multiple sortings* is the deep learning here.
problems.parent_script: Lay out a mix of sizes. **"Can you sort these?"** Don't tell them by what — see what they do.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Choosing size on their own (rather than color) → less common, valuable.
- Realizing they could sort the same set two different ways → developmental win.
problems.capture_field: Did they discover size as a sorting rule? Were they stuck thinking of color?

problems.title: Two ways to sort
problems.prompt: Lay them out mixed. **"Sort them however you want."** Let them sort (probably by color or size). Then say: **"That was great! Can you sort them a different way?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How is this way different from the first way?"** This is the core insight: the same objects can be organized two different ways depending on which attribute you attend to.
problems.parent_script: Lay them out mixed. **"Sort them however you want."** Let them sort (probably by color or size). Then say: **"That was great! Can you sort them a different way?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Sorting one way then the other → big abstract leap.
- Stuck on one way → fine. Suggest "what about by how big they are?"
problems.capture_field: Did they find both ways? What words did they use for each?

problems.title: The "is not" game
problems.prompt: Lay out 5 things. **"I'm thinking of one of these. It's not red. It's not made of metal. It's not soft."** Each clue narrows the field. **"Which one am I thinking of?"**
materials: 5 different small objects in plain view
problems.explain_prompt: **"Why did 'not red' help you?"** Negative clues are harder than positive ones; reasoning from absence is more abstract than from presence.
problems.parent_script: Lay out 5 things. **"I'm thinking of one of these. It's not red. It's not made of metal. It's not soft."** Each clue narrows the field. **"Which one am I thinking of?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They eliminate as you give clues → strong logical thinking.
- They get confused — fine, give positive clues mixed in ("it's round").
- Older or quicker kids will want to give you "is not" clues. Let them.
problems.capture_field: Did they eliminate as clues came? Any moment of "ohhh!"?

problems.title: Animal homes
problems.prompt: Lay out the animal pictures and the "home" labels. **"Where does each animal live?"** Sort them together: lion → jungle, fish → water, etc.
problems.explain_prompt: **"Why do you think the fish lives in the water?"** Categorical knowledge by function/habitat — a different kind of sorting than by visible attributes.
problems.parent_script: Lay out the animal pictures and the "home" labels. **"Where does each animal live?"** Sort them together: lion → jungle, fish → water, etc.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They sort confidently → solid background knowledge.
- "Frog → pond or water?" → ambiguity is fine. Discuss: frogs live both places.
- "What if a fish came out of water?" → wonderful conversation territory.
problems.capture_field: Any ambiguous sortings? Any surprising knowledge?

problems.title: What's missing?
problems.prompt: Put 4 objects in front of your child. **"Look closely. Remember what's here."** Have them close their eyes. Remove one. **"Open. What's missing?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you remember?"** Memory of specific items vs. memory of the *set* are different cognitive strategies.
problems.parent_script: Put 4 objects in front of your child. **"Look closely. Remember what's here."** Have them close their eyes. Remove one. **"Open. What's missing?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Quick recall of the missing one → strong attention.
- They name what's still there and figure out by elimination → also strong.
- A wrong guess → no big deal. Show them and try again.
problems.capture_field: Did they recall directly, or eliminate? Their words?

problems.title: Find the hidden rule
problems.prompt: You sort: put all the round things on the left, all the not-round on the right. **"I'm using a rule to sort these. Can you figure out my rule?"**
problems.explain_prompt: If they get it: **"Now you make a rule and I'll guess."** Inventing a rule is harder than discovering one.
problems.parent_script: You sort: put all the round things on the left, all the not-round on the right. **"I'm using a rule to sort these. Can you figure out my rule?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They notice the attribute → great.
- They notice but use the wrong word ("the puffy ones") → fine, you understand each other.
- They invent a different rule when it's their turn → exceptional.
problems.capture_field: Did they articulate your rule? What rule did they invent?

problems.title: Same shape, different size
problems.prompt: Mix them up. **"Can you put all the round ones together, and all the not-round ones together?"** When done, ask: **"Are all the round ones the same?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"They're different sizes — but they're all round. What makes them all round?"** Identifying the *shape* property regardless of size is a big abstraction.
problems.parent_script: Mix them up. **"Can you put all the round ones together, and all the not-round ones together?"** When done, ask: **"Are all the round ones the same?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They group by shape easily → shape recognition solid.
- Confusion when sizes vary widely → totally normal. Reassure: "yes, this big one and this little one are both circles."
problems.capture_field: What word did they use for "round"? Did size confuse them?

problems.title: The mirror game
problems.prompt: Sit facing your child. **"Pretend we're mirrors. When I move, you move the same way."** Lift your left arm — they lift their right (it mirrors yours). Touch your nose — they do. Move slowly.
problems.explain_prompt: Switch: they lead. **"Now you be the leader and I'll mirror."** Symmetry through embodiment.
problems.parent_script: Sit facing your child. **"Pretend we're mirrors. When I move, you move the same way."** Lift your left arm — they lift their right (it mirrors yours). Touch your nose — they do. Move slowly.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They naturally mirror (using opposite side) → spatial intuition.
- They copy literally (same side) → also fine, just different framing. Clarify if you want: "no, I'm the mirror — my right is your left."
problems.capture_field: Did they understand mirror vs. copy? What did they say if confused?

problems.title: Above, below, beside
problems.prompt: Put the toy *on top of* the cup. **"Where is the toy?"** They say "on top" or "above." Move it *under*. Move it *beside*. **"And now?"** Then: **"Put the toy under the chair. Beside the door. On top of your foot."**
problems.explain_prompt: **"Can you tell me where something is in this room — without pointing?"** Spatial language without gesture is harder.
problems.parent_script: Put the toy *on top of* the cup. **"Where is the toy?"** They say "on top" or "above." Move it *under*. Move it *beside*. **"And now?"** Then: **"Put the toy under the chair. Beside the door. On top of your foot."**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Vocabulary range: on / under / beside / behind / in front / between.
- "There" + pointing → very common at Pre-K. Push gently for words.
problems.capture_field: What spatial words did they have? Which were missing?

problems.title: Folded paper hearts
problems.prompt: Fold a paper in half. Draw half a heart shape against the fold. **"What do you think will happen when I cut it?"** Cut and unfold — full heart. Try again with half a butterfly, half a star.
problems.explain_prompt: **"What if we drew a circle on the fold? What would come out?"** Predicting before cutting is the geometric reasoning.
problems.parent_script: Fold a paper in half. Draw half a heart shape against the fold. **"What do you think will happen when I cut it?"** Cut and unfold — full heart. Try again with half a butterfly, half a star.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "It'll be a whole thing!" → they got the symmetry idea.
- Surprise at the result → also fine, the surprise is the learning.
- They want to try cutting themselves → great. Let them.
problems.capture_field: Did they predict correctly? What did they say about the symmetry?

problems.title: Build what I built
problems.prompt: Build a small structure with 4 blocks (e.g., 3 in a row on the bottom, one on top of the middle). Hide it briefly behind something so they see it for 3 seconds, then hide. **"Can you build the same thing?"**
problems.explain_prompt: When done, compare. **"Is yours the same as mine? What's different?"** Visual memory + spatial reconstruction.
problems.parent_script: Build a small structure with 4 blocks (e.g., 3 in a row on the bottom, one on top of the middle). Hide it briefly behind something so they see it for 3 seconds, then hide. **"Can you build the same thing?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Number of blocks right → counting and spatial memory working together.
- Wrong arrangement → discover differences together.
- The compare step is the key learning, not the build itself.
problems.capture_field: Did they reconstruct accurately? What did they spot when comparing?

problems.title: Match the shape
problems.prompt: **"Let's find five circles in our house."** Walk around together. Plates, doorknobs, faces of cans, buttons. Then: **"Let's find five squares."** Then triangles, then rectangles.
problems.explain_prompt: **"What's the difference between a square and a rectangle?"** This question is hard — squares are rectangles, but Pre-K kids usually see them as different. Their answer is interesting either way.
problems.parent_script: **"Let's find five circles in our house."** Walk around together. Plates, doorknobs, faces of cans, buttons. Then: **"Let's find five squares."** Then triangles, then rectangles.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Vocabulary: circle, square, triangle, rectangle.
- Finding shapes in unexpected places → strong shape recognition.
- The square/rectangle question may be too abstract — that's fine.
problems.capture_field: What was their best find? How did they distinguish square from rectangle?

problems.title: Half a face
problems.prompt: Draw half a face on a piece of paper — vertical line down the middle, then half a mouth, half a nose, one eye, on the left side only. Show it to your child. **"Can you draw the other half?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you know where to put the other eye?"** Symmetry through observation, not formula.
problems.parent_script: Draw half a face on a piece of paper — vertical line down the middle, then half a mouth, half a nose, one eye, on the left side only. Show it to your child. **"Can you draw the other half?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- They mirror placement correctly → strong spatial sense.
- One feature is off — fine. The drawing is the conversation.
- They draw two different eyes or add new features → creative, less symmetric. Acknowledge both options.
problems.capture_field: How accurate was the symmetry? Did they add their own features?

problems.title: Blocks behind your back
problems.prompt: Show all 4 objects. Have your child close eyes. Put one behind their back, into their hand. **"Without looking, what is it?"** They feel it. They guess.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you know it was the spoon?"** Tactile geometry — recognizing shape without sight.
problems.parent_script: Show all 4 objects. Have your child close eyes. Put one behind their back, into their hand. **"Without looking, what is it?"** They feel it. They guess.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "Because it has a long part" → describing shape by feel.
- "It's flat and round like a coin" → multi-attribute reasoning.
- A wrong guess → laugh, reveal, do it again.
problems.capture_field: What words did they use for the felt shape? Any surprises?

problems.title: Longer, shorter
problems.prompt: Pick two: a pencil and a spoon. Lay them side by side. **"Which is longer?"** They point. Try other pairs.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know it's longer? Can you show me?"** Aligning ends to compare is the foundational measurement act.
problems.parent_script: Pick two: a pencil and a spoon. Lay them side by side. **"Which is longer?"** They point. Try other pairs.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Aligning ends without prompting → mature comparison.
- Just looking → fine when difference is big, breaks down when close.
- "Same length" → strong, often the hardest call to make.
problems.capture_field: How did they compare? Did they align ends?

problems.title: Taller than the cat?
problems.prompt: Put a stuffed bear on the floor. **"Is the bear taller than the table? Than the door? Than your knee?"** Compare against each thing.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How can we check?"** They might suggest standing the bear next to the thing. That's the measurement principle in action.
problems.parent_script: Put a stuffed bear on the floor. **"Is the bear taller than the table? Than the door? Than your knee?"** Compare against each thing.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "We can put it next to" → measurement strategy.
- Just answering by sight → fine when difference is big.
- "Same!" for close calls → reasoning about equality of measure.
problems.capture_field: Did they propose how to check? What was their strategy?

problems.title: Heavy or light?
problems.prompt: Lay them out. **"Pick up each one. Which is heaviest? Which is lightest?"** Let them sort by weight, lightest to heaviest.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know the can is heavier than the block?"** Direct feel. Sometimes "I just know," sometimes "my hand goes down more."
problems.parent_script: Lay them out. **"Pick up each one. Which is heaviest? Which is lightest?"** Let them sort by weight, lightest to heaviest.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Confident ordering → solid weight intuition.
- Confusion between big/small and heavy/light → the misconception to gently surface. A small can vs. a big balloon: which is heavier?
problems.capture_field: Did size confuse them about weight?

problems.title: How many cups in this bowl?
problems.prompt: **"How many of these cups do you think will fit in this bowl?"** Make a guess together. Then fill. Count: "one, two, three …"
problems.explain_prompt: **"Was your guess right? Was it more or less?"** Estimation followed by measurement — the foundational pattern of practical math.
problems.parent_script: **"How many of these cups do you think will fit in this bowl?"** Make a guess together. Then fill. Count: "one, two, three …"
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- The guess matters less than the willingness to make one.
- Counting accurately while pouring is harder than you'd think.
- "Now let's try the big bowl" → estimation gets better with repetition.
problems.capture_field: What was their guess? How close were they?

problems.title: Cold or warm?
problems.prompt: Line up the 4 cups. **"Touch each one. Which is coldest? Which is hottest?"** Order them by temperature.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How would you describe this one to someone who couldn't feel it?"** Vocabulary for temperature: cold, cool, warm, hot. Plus "in between" feels good for the middle cups.
problems.parent_script: Line up the 4 cups. **"Touch each one. Which is coldest? Which is hottest?"** Order them by temperature.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Ordering correctly → temperature sense intact.
- Vocabulary range — how many words do they have?
- "In between" → comparing relatively, a real conceptual win.
problems.capture_field: What words did they use? Any "in between" reasoning?

problems.title: How long is a song?
problems.prompt: Sing "Twinkle Twinkle" together. **"Was that short or long?"** Then sing "Wheels on the Bus" with all the verses. **"Which song was longer?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How could we measure how long a song is?"** "Counting" comes up — counting verses, counting seconds, counting our steps while singing. Each is a valid unit.
problems.parent_script: Sing "Twinkle Twinkle" together. **"Was that short or long?"** Then sing "Wheels on the Bus" with all the verses. **"Which song was longer?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Time is hard at this age. "Longer" / "shorter" with felt experience is the goal.
- Inventing units (steps, claps) → developmental win.
problems.capture_field: Did they propose a unit? Which one?

problems.title: Where could they sit?
problems.prompt: Put 2 plates out. **"Two seats at the table. Here's Bear and Bunny. Where can each sit? Can you find all the ways?"** Let them place.
problems.explain_prompt: Once they find both arrangements: **"What if there were three friends — Bear, Bunny, Lion? How many ways then?"** Don't expect them to solve it. The leap of asking "what if" is the goal.
problems.parent_script: Put 2 plates out. **"Two seats at the table. Here's Bear and Bunny. Where can each sit? Can you find all the ways?"** Let them place.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Treating Bear-left/Bunny-right and Bear-right/Bunny-left as different ways → conservation of position.
- Trying 3 animals and intuiting more options → exceptional.
problems.capture_field: Two ways or one? Did they try the 3-animal extension?

problems.title: Two hats, one face
problems.prompt: Show two hats — say a red one and a blue one. **"You can wear one hat at a time. How many different ways can you wear a hat?"** Two ways (red, then blue).
problems.explain_prompt: **"What if you had three hats? How many ways?"** Three. **"What if you had a hat AND a scarf? Two hats, two scarves — how many outfits?"** Now it's 2 × 2 = 4 ways. Don't expect them to multiply — let them try every combination physically.
problems.parent_script: Show two hats — say a red one and a blue one. **"You can wear one hat at a time. How many different ways can you wear a hat?"** Two ways (red, then blue).
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Listing all 4 outfits physically → strong combinatorial sense.
- Listing only 2 or 3 → developmentally typical. Help them spot what they missed.
problems.capture_field: Did they find all 4 outfits? Which did they miss?

problems.title: Sock matching
problems.prompt: Dump 6 mixed socks in front of your child. **"Can you find the pairs?"** They sort.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you know these two match?"** Color, pattern, size — multiple attributes have to all line up for a "match."
problems.parent_script: Dump 6 mixed socks in front of your child. **"Can you find the pairs?"** They sort.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Matching by multi-attribute → real categorical reasoning.
- A "near miss" (similar but not exact) → discuss: "are these the same exactly? Or close but not exact?"
problems.capture_field: What attributes did they use to match? Any close-but-not-exact pairs?

problems.title: Three friends, three colors
problems.prompt: **"Each friend gets a bead. How many ways can we give them out?"** Let them physically try arrangements.
problems.explain_prompt: The full answer is 6 ways, but Pre-K kids will find 2–4. **"Are there more? Can you find a different way?"** The goal isn't completeness — it's the search.
problems.parent_script: **"Each friend gets a bead. How many ways can we give them out?"** Let them physically try arrangements.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Iterating to find new combinations → systematic thinking emerging.
- Repeating an arrangement and not noticing → fine. Help them track: "We already did red→Bear, blue→Bunny, yellow→Lion."
problems.capture_field: How many arrangements did they find? Did they get stuck?

problems.title: Pick-up sticks
problems.prompt: Lay out 5 sticks. **"We take turns. On your turn, you take 1 or 2 sticks. Whoever takes the last stick wins."** Play. Let them try various strategies.
problems.explain_prompt: After a few games: **"Have you noticed anything that helps you win?"** The winning strategy exists (take a multiple of 3) but Pre-K kids won't find it. Noticing *anything* — that some moves are better than others — is the goal.
problems.parent_script: Lay out 5 sticks. **"We take turns. On your turn, you take 1 or 2 sticks. Whoever takes the last stick wins."** Play. Let them try various strategies.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Trying different numbers of sticks → experimenting.
- "If I take one, I win" → forward thinking, even one move ahead.
- Wanting to play again → engagement.
problems.capture_field: Any strategy emerging? Any frustration?

problems.title: Race to ten
problems.prompt: Each player starts with no counters. Take turns rolling the die. Take that many counters. First to 10 wins.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How many more do you need to win?"** Subtraction in disguise. 10 minus current count.
problems.parent_script: Each player starts with no counters. Take turns rolling the die. Take that many counters. First to 10 wins.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counting their pile after each roll → maintaining a running total.
- "I need three more!" → mental subtraction in context.
problems.capture_field: Did they track the running total? Any mental arithmetic?

problems.title: Memory match
problems.prompt: Lay all 8 cards face down. Each turn, flip two cards. If they match (both show 3 dots), keep them. If not, flip back over. Take turns.
problems.explain_prompt: When they flip a card: **"How many dots? How do you know?"** Subitizing in a game wrapper.
problems.parent_script: Lay all 8 cards face down. Each turn, flip two cards. If they match (both show 3 dots), keep them. If not, flip back over. Take turns.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Subitizing 1–3 instantly, slower for 4.
- Memory for card positions → general working memory, not specifically math.
- Trying to remember "the 3 card was here" → strong pattern memory.
problems.capture_field: Subitizing speed? Memory for positions?

problems.title: Who has more?
problems.prompt: Deal one card to each player, face up. **"Whose number is bigger?"** Bigger number wins. Play 10 hands.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How much bigger is your 5 than my 2?"** Difference / "how many more" reasoning.
problems.parent_script: Deal one card to each player, face up. **"Whose number is bigger?"** Bigger number wins. Play 10 hands.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Quick comparison → solid number recognition.
- "How many more" — counting up, or subtracting? Both work.
- Ties → "we're the same! Same number!"
problems.capture_field: Comparison speed? Any "how many more" reasoning?

problems.title: Beat me to the top
problems.prompt: Both start at "Start." Take turns rolling the die, move that many squares. First to the top wins.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How many more squares do you need?"** Each turn — distance to finish. A natural subtraction-in-context.
problems.parent_script: Both start at "Start." Take turns rolling the die, move that many squares. First to the top wins.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Tracking "where am I, where are you, who's ahead?" — three-way comparison.
- "I need 4 more" → mental subtraction.
- The losing/winning emotion — math games can prompt early frustration. Practice graceful losing matters.
problems.capture_field: Distance-to-finish reasoning? Any emotional moments?

problems.title: The disappearing coin
problems.prompt: Put 4 coins on the table. **"Can you split these into two equal piles?"** Two and two — yes! Now 5 coins. **"Can you split these into two equal piles?"** No — one is left over. Try 6 (yes). Try 7 (no). Try 8 (yes).
problems.explain_prompt: **"Why does it work with some numbers and not others?"** They may not have the words "even" and "odd" yet — that's fine. The discovery that some quantities split fairly and some don't is the foundation.
problems.parent_script: Put 4 coins on the table. **"Can you split these into two equal piles?"** Two and two — yes! Now 5 coins. **"Can you split these into two equal piles?"** No — one is left over. Try 6 (yes). Try 7 (no). Try 8 (yes).
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Noticing the pattern (it works with 2, 4, 6, 8 but not 1, 3, 5, 7) → exceptional Pre-K reasoning.
- "There's always one left over!" → the parity insight in their own words.
- No pattern recognition → fine. Just play the game.
problems.capture_field: Did they notice the every-other pattern? Their words?

problems.title: Subitize 4 to 6
problems.prompt: Put 4 pebbles on the table, briefly cover and reveal as before. **"How many?"** Then 5. Then 6. Mix the order. The arrangement matters — sometimes line them up, sometimes cluster them, sometimes spread them.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you see it so fast?"** At Level 2 we're listening for *part-whole strategies*: "I saw 3 and 3" for 6, "4 and 1 more" for 5. That's a big developmental leap from raw subitizing.
problems.parent_script: Put 4 pebbles on the table, briefly cover and reveal as before. **"How many?"** Then 5. Then 6. Mix the order. The arrangement matters — sometimes line them up, sometimes cluster them, sometimes spread them.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "Three and three" / "two and four" → decomposing on the fly. Late-Pre-K marker.
- Counting one-by-one → fine, but slower. Try again with the same arrangement next session.
- Confident 4 and 5 but slower on 6 → totally normal; 6 is the upper subitizing edge at this age.
problems.capture_field: Did they decompose ("I saw 3 and 3") or count? Which numbers were instant vs. counted?

problems.title: Count to 10 with matching
problems.prompt: Lay out 10 objects in a row. **"Let's count them — touch each one as we say a number."** Touch and count together to 10. Then: **"Your turn. I'll just listen."**
problems.explain_prompt: **"What number comes after 7? And after 9?"** Naming the next number without counting from 1 is what we're working toward. Some kids will count internally first — fine.
problems.parent_script: Lay out 10 objects in a row. **"Let's count them — touch each one as we say a number."** Touch and count together to 10. Then: **"Your turn. I'll just listen."**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Reliable 1–10 with one-to-one matching → solid.
- Skipping a number (1, 2, 3, 5...) → very common; gentle correction by counting together again.
- Knowing "after 7 is 8" without restarting → strong number-line intuition emerging.
problems.capture_field: Did they count up to 10 cleanly? Could they name the number after 7 without restarting?

problems.title: Count backward from 10
problems.prompt: Put 10 raisins out. **"We're going to eat them one at a time, counting backward. Ready? Ten … nine … eight …"** Eat (or move aside) one per number. Together at first; let them carry it solo on the second round.
problems.explain_prompt: **"What comes before 5? What comes before 1?"** Backward counting is significantly harder than forward — predicting one *before* is a real cognitive lift.
problems.parent_script: Put 10 raisins out. **"We're going to eat them one at a time, counting backward. Ready? Ten … nine … eight …"** Eat (or move aside) one per number. Together at first; let them carry it solo on the second round.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- 10 down to 5 clean, stumbles below → normal. Practice over weeks.
- "Before 1 is zero" → conceptual win.
- "Before 1 is nothing" or shrug → fine. Zero comes later for most.
problems.capture_field: How far did they count backward cleanly? Their word for "before 1"?

problems.title: Close call: 4 or 5?
problems.prompt: Make two piles: 4 on the left, 5 on the right. **"Which has more?"** Don't make it obvious — keep the piles visually similar. Repeat with 5 vs. 6, 6 vs. 7.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How do you know it's more? Can you prove it?"** "Prove it" elicits the pairing or counting strategy. Just looking won't work when piles are close.
problems.parent_script: Make two piles: 4 on the left, 5 on the right. **"Which has more?"** Don't make it obvious — keep the piles visually similar. Repeat with 5 vs. 6, 6 vs. 7.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Pairs them off physically → mature strategy.
- Counts both piles → also mature.
- Visual judgment that turns out wrong → discovery moment. "Let's pair them up and see."
problems.capture_field: Which strategy did they use? Did they realize visual judgment fails for close calls?

problems.title: The next number game
problems.prompt: **"I'll say a number, and you tell me the next one."** Start with 1 → 2. Then 5 → 6. Then 7 → 8. Then jump to 9 → 10. Then 0 → 1.
problems.explain_prompt: **"And what comes two after 5?"** Skip-count by 1 twice — "5 → 6 → 7." Working memory and the number-line concept getting exercised.
problems.parent_script: **"I'll say a number, and you tell me the next one."** Start with 1 → 2. Then 5 → 6. Then 7 → 8. Then jump to 9 → 10. Then 0 → 1.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Instant "after 5 is 6" → solid number-line internalization.
- Restarting from 1 ("one, two, three, four, five, six!") → developmental and fine.
- "Two after 5 is 7" without restarting → exceptional.
problems.capture_field: Could they name "next" without restarting? How about "two after"?

problems.title: Five in many ways
problems.prompt: **"Show me 5 fingers."** Most kids do one whole hand. **"That's one way! Can you show me 5 a different way?"** Encourage 4+1, 3+2. Then ask for 6, 7, 8 the same way (each across two hands).
problems.explain_prompt: **"How many different ways can you show 5?"** Decomposing 5 systematically (4+1, 3+2, 2+3, 1+4, 5+0) is the foundation of number bonds — the K core concept.
problems.parent_script: **"Show me 5 fingers."** Most kids do one whole hand. **"That's one way! Can you show me 5 a different way?"** Encourage 4+1, 3+2. Then ask for 6, 7, 8 the same way (each across two hands).
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- One way → developmentally typical Pre-K.
- Two or three ways → late-Pre-K marker. Strong.
- Five ways (including 5+0 and asymmetric pairs) → K-ready thinking.
problems.capture_field: How many different ways did they find? Which were intuitive vs. effortful?

problems.title: Order them, least to most
problems.prompt: Lay out 4 plates with different amounts. **"Can you put them in order, smallest pile to biggest?"** Let them work physically.
problems.explain_prompt: When they're done: **"How did you decide which was smallest? Which was biggest?"** Multi-way comparison is harder than pairwise.
problems.parent_script: Lay out 4 plates with different amounts. **"Can you put them in order, smallest pile to biggest?"** Let them work physically.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counting each pile, then ordering → strong process.
- Eyeballing for the extremes (biggest/smallest), counting the middle → very mature.
- Misorderings → discuss: "let's count them again, side by side."
problems.capture_field: Did they count each? Did they get the ordering right? Where did mistakes happen?

problems.title: Quick-look 5 and 6
problems.prompt: Put 5 stones out, cover them, lift for 1 second, cover again. **"How many?"** Then 6. Mix it up. Vary the layout: line, cluster, scattered.
problems.explain_prompt: **"Was it easier when they were in a line, or scattered?"** Layout dramatically affects subitizing. Noticing this is metacognition emerging.
problems.parent_script: Put 5 stones out, cover them, lift for 1 second, cover again. **"How many?"** Then 6. Mix it up. Vary the layout: line, cluster, scattered.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Instant 5 in a line, slower scattered → typical pattern.
- Decomposing scattered ("I saw 3 and 2") → late-Pre-K.
- Frustration with 6 → 6 is the absolute upper limit of typical subitizing; OK to keep at 5.
problems.capture_field: Did layout matter? What did they say about how they "saw" it?

problems.title: More by how many?
problems.prompt: Make 3 on the left, 5 on the right. **"Which is more? How many more?"** They might say "this one" without quantifying the difference. Press: "Yes, more — but how many *more*?"
problems.explain_prompt: **"How could we figure out how many more?"** Pair off matching items; what's left over is the difference.
problems.parent_script: Make 3 on the left, 5 on the right. **"Which is more? How many more?"** They might say "this one" without quantifying the difference. Press: "Yes, more — but how many *more*?"
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Pairs off and counts leftover → mature comparison strategy.
- Counts both and subtracts in their head → very advanced.
- "More, but I don't know how many more" → fine, suggest pairing.
problems.capture_field: Could they quantify the difference? What strategy did they use?

problems.title: The "what comes after" hop
problems.prompt: Mark 0–10 on the floor with tape. **"Hop to 4."** They hop. **"Now hop forward two — where are you?"** Count the hops aloud. Then back two: "where are you now?" Try other starts.
materials: chalk marks for a number line 0–10
problems.explain_prompt: **"What if you hop forward three from 6?"** Use the physical number line — they should walk it and check. Number-line reasoning grounded in the body.
problems.parent_script: Mark 0–10 on the floor with tape. **"Hop to 4."** They hop. **"Now hop forward two — where are you?"** Count the hops aloud. Then back two: "where are you now?" Try other starts.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Hopping accurately by count → embodied number-line forming.
- "From 6, three hops is 9" without hopping → mental number line developing.
- Going past 10 → discuss: "what comes after 10?" Eleven. New territory.
problems.capture_field: Did they need to physically hop, or could they reason without it?

problems.title: Two more, two less
problems.prompt: Line up 3 bears. **"How many? Now add two more."** Pause for them to do it. **"How many now?"** Then take 2 away. **"And now?"** Continue with different starts.
problems.explain_prompt: **"You started with 3, added 2, and got 5. How did you know it was 5?"** Listen for counting all vs. counting on vs. just knowing.
problems.parent_script: Line up 3 bears. **"How many? Now add two more."** Pause for them to do it. **"How many now?"** Then take 2 away. **"And now?"** Continue with different starts.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Recounts all → still typical at Pre-K.
- "Three… four, five" (counts on by 2) → emerging late-Pre-K strategy.
- "Three plus two is five" without counting → K-ready.
problems.capture_field: How did they get to 5 from 3+2? Their actual method?

problems.title: Count on from here
problems.prompt: Hold up 4 fingers. **"This is 4. Don't count them — just remember: 4."** Then hold up 2 more on the other hand. **"How many altogether?"** The goal is for them to say "five, six" rather than "one, two, three, four, five, six."
problems.explain_prompt: **"You didn't start at one this time. You started at four. Why?"** Naming the strategy — "I already knew it was 4 so I started there" — is a real metacognitive win.
problems.parent_script: Hold up 4 fingers. **"This is 4. Don't count them — just remember: 4."** Then hold up 2 more on the other hand. **"How many altogether?"** The goal is for them to say "five, six" rather than "one, two, three, four, five, six."
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counts on from 4 → late-Pre-K marker. Excellent.
- Still starts from 1 → fine; the strategy comes with practice.
- Says "5, 6" out loud → they're vocalizing the count-on. Encourage.
problems.capture_field: Could they count on, or did they restart? Their words for the strategy?

problems.title: Take from 7
problems.prompt: Put 7 pebbles out. Count them together. **"Take away 3."** They remove 3. **"How many are left?"** Then try: start with 7, take 5. Then 7, take 1.
problems.explain_prompt: **"You started with 7 and took 3, and got 4. Is there a way to know that without recounting?"** Some kids will spot the pattern (7 → 6, 5, 4, three steps back).
problems.parent_script: Put 7 pebbles out. Count them together. **"Take away 3."** They remove 3. **"How many are left?"** Then try: start with 7, take 5. Then 7, take 1.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Recounts the leftover → standard.
- Counts down from 7: "six, five, four" while taking → strong subtraction-as-counting-back.
- "Seven take three is four" without doing it physically → exceptional.
problems.capture_field: Did they have to recount, or work it out by counting back?

problems.title: Combine two groups
problems.prompt: Make two piles: 3 on the left, 4 on the right. **"How many altogether?"** Let them work — they might push together, count both, count on.
problems.explain_prompt: **"Is there a way to know without counting them all?"** Listen for counting-on: "four… five, six, seven." Or known facts: "three plus four is seven."
problems.parent_script: Make two piles: 3 on the left, 4 on the right. **"How many altogether?"** Let them work — they might push together, count both, count on.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Pushes them together and counts all 7 → typical.
- Counts on from 4 → late-Pre-K.
- "Three and four is seven" → ready for K.
problems.capture_field: What strategy did they pick? Did it change across the rounds?

problems.title: Seven in many ways
problems.prompt: Show 7 pennies. **"Can you split these into two piles? Any way you like."** They split. Note the split: e.g. 3 + 4. **"Can you split them a different way?"** Continue until they're tired.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How many different ways can we split 7?"** Don't expect them to find all 6; finding 3–4 is great. Number bonds for 7 in physical form.
problems.parent_script: Show 7 pennies. **"Can you split these into two piles? Any way you like."** They split. Note the split: e.g. 3 + 4. **"Can you split them a different way?"** Continue until they're tired.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Two different splits → developmental win.
- Treating 3+4 and 4+3 as the same → mature.
- Treating them as different → also fine; commutativity is a later insight.
problems.capture_field: How many splits did they find? Did they spot 3+4 vs 4+3 as same/different?

problems.title: Under the cup, with 7
problems.prompt: Show 7 pennies. Have them count to 7. Split: some under cup A, some under cup B (you choose: say 3 and 4). Lift cup A: 3. **"How many under the other cup? How do you know?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you figure that out?"** The missing-addend logic — 7 total, 3 visible, must be 4 hidden — is a key K concept emerging early.
problems.parent_script: Show 7 pennies. Have them count to 7. Split: some under cup A, some under cup B (you choose: say 3 and 4). Lift cup A: 3. **"How many under the other cup? How do you know?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "Because 3 and 4 is 7" → reasoning structurally.
- "Because I counted 7 and saw 3, so it's the rest" → counting-based.
- A guess → reveal, recount together, try again with a different split.
problems.capture_field: Reasoning or guessing? What reasoning, if any?

problems.title: Two-step story
problems.prompt: **"There are 5 ducks in the pond. Two more ducks fly in."** Have them count: 7. **"Then 3 ducks fly away."** They count: 4. **"How many ducks are left?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"Did anyone count? Or did you just know each time?"** Two-step problems require holding intermediate state — a working-memory exercise.
problems.parent_script: **"There are 5 ducks in the pond. Two more ducks fly in."** Have them count: 7. **"Then 3 ducks fly away."** They count: 4. **"How many ducks are left?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Acts it out physically → strong support strategy.
- Tracks counts in their head → late-Pre-K to early-K.
- Loses track → totally fine; redo with smaller starts (3 + 2 - 1).
problems.capture_field: Could they track two steps? Where did they lose the thread, if anywhere?

problems.title: Backwards story
problems.prompt: **"There were some animals at the park. Three went home. Now there are 4 left. How many were there at the start?"** Hard. Have them act it out — start with 4 (the leftover), add 3 back.
problems.explain_prompt: **"You worked backwards. What did you have to figure out?"** Reasoning from the result is the seed of algebra.
problems.parent_script: **"There were some animals at the park. Three went home. Now there are 4 left. How many were there at the start?"** Hard. Have them act it out — start with 4 (the leftover), add 3 back.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Acting it out and recounting → strong.
- "Seven, because 4 plus 3 is 7" → exceptional.
- Stuck → no shame. This is hard. Try with 2 + 2 = 4 instead.
problems.capture_field: Could they reason backwards? What made it click, or where did they get stuck?

problems.title: Match my pile of 8
problems.prompt: Make a pile of 8 in front of you. **"Can you make a pile the same size as mine?"** Let them work. Then ask how they know.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How can you be sure they're the same without counting?"** Pairing off — lining one of theirs against one of yours — is the equality-as-relation insight.
problems.parent_script: Make a pile of 8 in front of you. **"Can you make a pile the same size as mine?"** Let them work. Then ask how they know.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Counting up to 8 in their pile → solid strategy.
- Pairing one-to-one → equality concept very strong.
- "About the same" by eyeball with 8 each → push for verification.
problems.capture_field: Counted or paired? Confident in their answer?

problems.title: Three on each side
problems.prompt: Put 3 pennies on one side of the balance. **"How many on the other side to balance it?"** They guess — let them add one at a time. **"Tell me when it's balanced."**
problems.explain_prompt: **"Could it be balanced with fewer? With more?"** The "same amount of stuff" idea is foundational; will fail interestingly when objects have different weights, which is fine to explore.
problems.parent_script: Put 3 pennies on one side of the balance. **"How many on the other side to balance it?"** They guess — let them add one at a time. **"Tell me when it's balanced."**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Adds three one at a time → strong iteration.
- Adds two and notices it's "not enough" → strong visual/physical feedback.
- "It has to be three because it's three on the other side" → equality reasoning.
problems.capture_field: Could they articulate why it balanced at three?

problems.title: Take one from each
problems.prompt: Make two equal piles: 5 and 5. **"Same?"** Yes. **"Now I take one from this pile."** Take one. **"Are they still the same?"** Then: put it back. Take one from each. **"Now?"** Still same!
problems.explain_prompt: **"Why is it still the same after I took one from each? But not after I took one from only one?"** This is the "balanced operations" idea — the foundation of solving equations someday.
problems.parent_script: Make two equal piles: 5 and 5. **"Same?"** Yes. **"Now I take one from this pile."** Take one. **"Are they still the same?"** Then: put it back. Take one from each. **"Now?"** Still same!
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "Because they both lost one" → strong relational thinking.
- Confused → totally fine. Demonstrate with smaller piles (2 and 2).
- Aha moment → big developmental win, often visible.
problems.capture_field: Did they get the "take from each = still equal" idea? In what words?

problems.title: Make them fair
problems.prompt: Plate A has 6 raisins. Plate B has 5. **"They're not fair. Can you make them fair?"** They might split the extra (impossible without breaking), move one over (making 5 and 6 → uneven again), or eat one. All teach something.
problems.explain_prompt: **"What did you have to do? Is there another way to make them fair?"** Multiple solutions exist (one eaten, one set aside, one split).
problems.parent_script: Plate A has 6 raisins. Plate B has 5. **"They're not fair. Can you make them fair?"** They might split the extra (impossible without breaking), move one over (making 5 and 6 → uneven again), or eat one. All teach something.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Sets one aside → understands fairness as equality.
- Moves one from A to B → ends up with 5 and 6 again. Discovery: "still not fair!"
- Wants to break/split → great, but discuss: "raisins don't really split. What else could we do?"
problems.capture_field: What approaches did they try? Any failed attempts that led to insight?

problems.title: ABCABC three-color
problems.prompt: Build a pattern: **red, blue, yellow, red, blue, yellow, red, blue, ...** **"What comes next?"** They predict. Continue: **"And after that?"** Then a different one: **red, red, blue, red, red, blue, ...**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How would you describe this pattern to someone who couldn't see it?"** Articulating a three-element rule in words is harder than two.
problems.parent_script: Build a pattern: **red, blue, yellow, red, blue, yellow, red, blue, ...** **"What comes next?"** They predict. Continue: **"And after that?"** Then a different one: **red, red, blue, red, red, blue, ...**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Confident prediction across the cycle → solid grasp.
- Predicts correctly but can't say the rule → typical. Words follow understanding.
- Verbalizes "red blue yellow keeps coming again" → strong articulation.
problems.capture_field: Could they describe a 3-color rule in words?

problems.title: AABB doubled pattern
problems.prompt: Build: **red, red, blue, blue, red, red, blue, blue, ...** **"What comes next?"** AABB feels different from ABAB. Many kids predict ABAB by reflex; let them and see.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How is this pattern different from red-blue-red-blue?"** Comparing two patterns surfaces the structural difference.
problems.parent_script: Build: **red, red, blue, blue, red, red, blue, blue, ...** **"What comes next?"** AABB feels different from ABAB. Many kids predict ABAB by reflex; let them and see.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Predicts "red, red" → caught the doubling.
- Predicts "blue" → reflex from ABAB. Reveal "red, red" and discuss.
- Builds their own AABB → exceptional.
problems.capture_field: Did they notice the doubling? Could they make their own AABB?

problems.title: Big-red, small-blue
problems.prompt: Build the pattern, mixing two attributes that change together. **"What comes next?"** They predict — both size and color have to be right.
materials: Objects varying in size AND color — e.g
problems.explain_prompt: **"What two things change every time?"** Surfacing the two-attribute structure is a real abstraction step.
problems.parent_script: Build the pattern, mixing two attributes that change together. **"What comes next?"** They predict — both size and color have to be right.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Gets size right, color wrong → tracking one attribute.
- Both right → tracking two. Late-Pre-K marker.
- Articulates "it goes big red, then small blue" → strong verbal grasp.
problems.capture_field: Could they track both attributes? Did they verbalize the rule?

problems.title: Predict three ahead
problems.prompt: Build: **red, blue, red, blue, red.** **"What comes next?"** They say blue. **"And after that?"** Red. **"And after that?"** Blue. Three predictions deep.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How could you know the eighth one without doing it one at a time?"** Some kids will start counting (1-red, 2-blue, 3-red, 4-blue) — that's the pattern-extending strategy at work.
problems.parent_script: Build: **red, blue, red, blue, red.** **"What comes next?"** They say blue. **"And after that?"** Red. **"And after that?"** Blue. Three predictions deep.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Three correct predictions → solid.
- Loses track at the second or third → working memory limit. Build it physically while they predict.
- Computes "the 8th is blue" by rule → exceptional.
problems.capture_field: How far ahead could they predict? Any signs of "rule-based" thinking vs. step-by-step?

problems.title: Growing snake
problems.prompt: Build rows of blocks: 1, then next to it 2, then 3, then 4. **"Look at our snake. What's the rule?"** Then ask them to build the 5th and 6th rows.
problems.explain_prompt: **"How many in the 7th row? Can you tell without building it?"** Counting forward through a growing pattern is real mathematical reasoning.
problems.parent_script: Build rows of blocks: 1, then next to it 2, then 3, then 4. **"Look at our snake. What's the rule?"** Then ask them to build the 5th and 6th rows.
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- "Seven, because it goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7" → strong.
- Builds it first to check → also strong, more grounded.
- "One more than the row before" articulated → captured the rule.
problems.capture_field: Could they articulate the +1 rule? Could they predict ahead?

problems.title: Find the mistake
problems.prompt: Build a pattern but slip in a mistake: **red, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, red.** (Note the two blues in a row.) **"There's a mistake in this pattern. Can you find it?"**
problems.explain_prompt: **"How did you know that was the mistake?"** They have to internalize the rule to spot the violation.
problems.parent_script: Build a pattern but slip in a mistake: **red, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, red.** (Note the two blues in a row.) **"There's a mistake in this pattern. Can you find it?"**
problems.what_to_listen_for:
- Finds the two-blues → strong pattern internalization.
- Points to a different spot → fine, ask "why?" — they might have a different mental model.
- Can't find it → walk through with them: "red, blue, red, blue, blue — wait."
problems.capture_field: Did they spot the mistake? Their explanation?

problems.title: Clap-stomp into blocks
problems.prompt: Do a clap-stomp pattern with sound: **clap, stomp, clap, stomp, clap, stomp.** **"Can you build that same pattern with these blocks? Use red for clap and blue for stomp."**
problems.explain_prompt: **"What if the pattern were clap-clap-stomp? How would the blocks look?"** Translating between modalities (audio → visual) tests structural understanding.
